What happened in the Nanjing massacre?

The Nanjing Massacre, also called the Rape of Nanjing, was a mass atrocity committed by Imperial Japanese Army forces after they captured Nanjing, then China’s capital, on December 13, 1937, during the Second Sino-Japanese War.

Over roughly six weeks, Japanese troops killed large numbers of Chinese civilians and disarmed soldiers, including many prisoners of war. They also carried out widespread rape, torture, looting, and destruction of property. Women and girls were particularly targeted in mass sexual violence.

The exact death toll remains debated because of incomplete records and differing methodologies. Estimates commonly range from well over 100,000 to about 300,000 victims; the International Military Tribunal for the Far East cited more than 200,000 killings, while Chinese official commemorations commonly cite 300,000. Regardless of the precise number, historians broadly agree it was one of the worst wartime atrocities of the 20th century.

Foreign residents, missionaries, and diplomats created the Nanjing Safety Zone, which sheltered many civilians and produced important contemporary documentation of the violence. The massacre remains a deeply sensitive subject in China and Japan, partly because of disputes over remembrance, responsibility, and historical denial or minimization.

What happened in the Nanjing massacre?

The Nanjing Massacre, also called the Rape of Nanking, was a mass atrocity committed by the Imperial Japanese Army after it captured Nanjing—then China’s capital—on December 13, 1937, during the Second Sino-Japanese War.

Over roughly six weeks, Japanese troops killed large numbers of Chinese civilians and disarmed soldiers, including through mass executions. They also carried out widespread rape, torture, looting, and arson. Civilians were targeted even though many had sought refuge in an internationally administered Safety Zone within the city.

The precise death toll is debated because wartime records are incomplete and estimates use different geographic and time boundaries. Major historical estimates range from well over 100,000 to about 300,000 victims; the figure of 300,000 is officially commemorated in China. There is broad scholarly consensus that large-scale atrocities occurred, supported by contemporary diaries, photographs, burial records, diplomatic reports, survivor testimony, and Japanese military-related evidence.

After the war, Japanese military leaders were prosecuted in international and Chinese war-crimes trials. The massacre remains a deeply painful issue in Chinese-Japanese relations, especially where denial or minimization of the atrocities occurs.
